questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a density-independent factor acting on a surveyed population
questions.stem: A field biologist records a colony of ground squirrels collapsing within a week of an unusually late snowstorm.

options.text: The snowstorm buried food and froze burrows regardless of how crowded the colony was
Parasitic wasps found the colony because the enlarged tunnels made hosts easier to locate
options.misconception: assumes parasite pressure scales with crowding

options.text: A bacterial disease spread through the colony as contact rates between adults rose
options.misconception: treats a disease outbreak as density independent

options.text: Competition for buried seeds intensified as the colony grew denser that season
options.misconception: reads crowding effects as the cause of the crash

questions.explanation: A snowstorm acts on a population whatever its density, so it is density independent. Crowding effects such as competition and disease strengthen as the population becomes denser.
questions.hint: Ask whether crowding affected the factor.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how far a population sits below its carrying capacity
questions.stem: A survey of a grassland vole population counted 480 individuals in March and 720 in September, against a carrying capacity of 900. By how many individuals does the September count fall short of the carrying capacity?
questions.explanation: The September count of 720 falls short of the carrying capacity of 900 by 180 individuals. A population below capacity can still grow, since resources are not yet fully used.
questions.hint: Subtract the counted population from the carrying capacity.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate proposals to raise the maximum size of a surveyed population
questions.stem: A reserve manager proposes adding nesting boxes to raise the maximum number of songbirds the marsh can hold.

options.text: Boxes may raise the carrying capacity, but per capita growth still slows as the birds approach it
Adding boxes lifts the carrying capacity and removes every other limit on the birds
options.misconception: assumes one new resource removes all other limiting factors

options.text: Boxes change the carrying capacity not at all, because it is fixed by the marsh area alone
options.misconception: believes carrying capacity depends on area only

options.text: Boxes remove the density-dependent limits and so let the population grow without bound
options.misconception: confuses raising capacity with removing limits entirely

questions.explanation: In logistic growth a population settles at the carrying capacity, so nest sites can raise that ceiling. The per capita growth rate still falls as the population nears it.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to per capita growth near the limit.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compute net population change from births, deaths and movement
questions.stem: Survey data for a badger population record 120 cubs born, 90 adults lost to mortality, 30 immigrants and 40 emigrants in one year.

options.text: The population grew by 200, because the birth total alone was counted as the change
options.misconception: ignores deaths and movement when computing change

options.text: The population grew by 30, because immigrants were added but deaths and emigration were ignored
options.misconception: counts movement but leaves out mortality

options.text: The population was stable, because births and deaths were roughly balanced each year
options.misconception: looks only at births against deaths and ignores movement

options.text: The population grew by 20, since births plus immigration exceeded deaths plus emigration

questions.explanation: Adding births and immigration gives 150 animals entering the population, and deaths plus emigration gives 130 leaving it. The net change is therefore a gain of 20 individuals over the year.
questions.hint: Total all the gains and subtract all the losses.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how migration changes a local population count
questions.stem: Counts of a coastal bird colony rise sharply each autumn, and the field team wants to know whether the birds bred there.

options.text: The birds are local breeders, because an autumn count proves young were produced there
options.misconception: reads a seasonal rise as evidence of local breeding

options.text: The birds are immigrants arriving from other coasts to overwinter, not local breeders
The birds are local breeders, since breeding colonies always peak in the autumn season
options.misconception: assumes a fixed breeding season for coastal birds

options.text: The birds are visitors from inland wetlands that use the coast only as a stopover
options.misconception: picks one alternative source without evidence for it

questions.explanation: A sharp autumn rise reflects birds arriving from elsewhere rather than a local birth pulse. Migration can raise a local count without changing the breeding population.
questions.hint: Think about when young birds appear in the breeding season.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate net change from births, deaths and emigration
questions.stem: During one year a surveyed badger population produced 11 cubs and lost 9 adults to mortality and emigration. What was the net change in the number of badgers?
questions.explanation: Full accounting pairs every gain with every loss, so 11 births minus 9 losses gives a net gain of 2 badgers. With no immigrants or emigrants recorded, movement must be stated explicitly.
questions.hint: Subtract the losses from the births.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why only a small share of energy passes between trophic levels
questions.stem: A survey of a lake finds that fish biomass greatly exceeds the biomass of the plankton they graze on.

options.text: The plankton must have been eaten by something else, because grazers always exceed their food
options.misconception: assumes grazer biomass must always be below the food biomass

options.text: The fish are eating something other than plankton, since only plankton was sampled
options.misconception: blames incomplete sampling for a real energy pattern

options.text: The fish biomass was measured with an error, because standing crops never exceed their food supply
options.misconception: assumes standing crop cannot exceed the stock it feeds on

options.text: Plankton can be replaced quickly by growth, so a small standing crop can support a large grazer crop

questions.explanation: A small standing biomass of plankton can support a much larger consumer biomass if the plankton is replaced quickly. Standing crop reflects turnover as well as size, so inversion is possible.
questions.hint: Consider how quickly the plankton population renews itself.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a productivity figure for a surveyed plot
questions.stem: A field plot produced 1,200 grams of plant dry matter per square metre per year and used 400 grams in plant respiration.

options.text: Net primary productivity is 800 grams, which is the material left after respiration
Net primary productivity is 1,200 grams, because dry matter totals the net production
options.misconception: confuses gross production with net production

options.text: Net primary productivity is 400 grams, since that is the total the plants respired
options.misconception: reports the respiratory loss as the net production

options.text: Net primary productivity is 1,600 grams, because respiration adds to the plant material produced
options.misconception: adds respiratory losses instead of subtracting them

questions.explanation: Net primary productivity is gross production minus what the plants respire, so 1,200 minus 400 gives 800 grams per square metre per year. That is new material available to grazers.
questions.hint: Subtract the respiratory use from the total produced.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Infer the energy at a lower level from a higher trophic level
questions.stem: A survey estimates 500 kilojoules of energy held in a marsh's herons, and the team wants the plant energy behind it.

options.text: About 500,000 kilojoules, since herons sit three steps above the plants in the food chain
About 5 kilojoules, because the herons are only two levels above the plants
options.misconception: misstates how many levels separate herons from plants

options.text: About 50,000 kilojoules, since each level up the pyramid adds rather than loses energy
options.misconception: believes energy increases as it moves up the pyramid

options.text: About 500 kilojoules, because energy is conserved from plants to herons as biomass
options.misconception: assumes energy is conserved between trophic levels

questions.explanation: Working backward means multiplying by ten at each step down, since only a tenth of energy passes up per level. From herons to plants is three steps, so 500 kilojoules implies 500,000.
questions.hint: Multiply by ten for each step back down the pyramid.

questions.learningObjective: Quantify the link to species ratio of a surveyed food web
questions.stem: A survey charted 12 feeding links among the 5 species recorded in a small drainage ditch. What is the mean number of feeding links per species?
questions.explanation: Web complexity can be described by the mean number of links each species carries, here 12 links over 5 species, or 2.4 links each. More links per species means more energy pathways.
questions.hint: Divide the number of links by the number of species.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish independent limits from crowding effects in field data
questions.stem: A surveyor blames a rodent fall on crowding, then finds the drop matched a week of extreme heat.

options.text: Crowding is the better explanation, because heat only hurts animals in poor condition
options.misconception: assumes heat damage depends on crowding

options.text: The heat is the better explanation, because it hit every density of the population alike
Both causes are equally likely, so the survey cannot rank the two explanations
options.misconception: refuses to weigh evidence between two competing causes

options.text: The heat is the better explanation, because heat is the only factor that can ever kill animals
options.misconception: treats one factor as the only possible cause of death

questions.explanation: A factor that operates the same way whatever the density is density independent, and extreme heat fits that pattern. Crowding effects would grow in strength as the population became denser.
questions.hint: Ask whether the factor's effect depends on crowding.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a population that is growing while below capacity
questions.stem: Survey counts for a pond fish population rise from 300 to 600 in a year, and the pond can support 1,200 fish.

options.text: The population has reached capacity, because the count doubled within a single year
options.misconception: confuses a doubling of numbers with reaching a limit

options.text: The population is doomed to crash, because any growth must be followed by a fall
options.misconception: assumes every increase must reverse immediately

options.text: The population is at capacity, since the fish are clearly using every resource available
options.misconception: claims a rising count proves the capacity limit is reached

options.text: The population is growing below capacity, with resources still left to support more fish

questions.explanation: A population below its carrying capacity keeps growing because resources are not yet used up, and 600 fish against 1,200 capacity is exactly that. The doubling rate says nothing about the ceiling.
questions.hint: Compare the count with the stated carrying capacity.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the defining feature of logistic growth
questions.stem: A biologist describes the way a reintroduced beaver population settled on a new river system.

options.text: The population grew quickly at first, then more slowly as it approached the habitat's limit
The population grew at a constant rate until it reached the habitat's limits and then stopped
options.misconception: describes linear growth and ignores slowing near capacity

options.text: The population grew only after the habitat was fully used by other species
options.misconception: assumes growth waits until others take the resources

options.text: The population grew fastest once it had passed the point where food became scarce
options.misconception: claims the growth rate peaks after resources are limiting

questions.explanation: Logistic growth rises steeply when the population is small and slows as the habitat fills, because competition intensifies. The curve levels off at the carrying capacity.
questions.hint: Think about how competition changes as the population grows.

questions.stem: A gull colony held 250 adult gulls at the start of the season, 84 chicks fledged and 31 adult gulls died. How many gulls were present at the end of the season?
questions.explanation: Adding 84 fledged chicks to 250 adults and subtracting 31 deaths gives 303 gulls at the end of the season. Full accounting needs both the young that join and the adults that leave.
questions.hint: Add the young, then subtract the adults that died.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about how migration confounds a local population count
questions.stem: A warden's claim that a local bird colony is thriving rests on counts that include passing migrants.

options.text: The claim is supported, because more birds on site always means a larger breeding colony
options.misconception: assumes a site count always reflects breeding numbers

options.text: The claim is unsupported, because passing migrants inflate the count without adding to the colony
The claim is supported, because migrants usually settle and join the breeding population
options.misconception: assumes all visiting birds become breeders

options.text: The claim is unsupported, because migrants prevent the colony from ever using its habitat
options.misconception: overstates the effect of migrants on habitat use

questions.explanation: Migrants inflate a local count without adding to the breeding population, so a count mixing residents with visitors cannot show colony growth. Counts of returning breeders are needed.
questions.hint: Separate resident birds from passing visitors.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Account for a population change including all four components
questions.stem: A year of survey data for a wood mouse population shows 400 births, 250 deaths, 60 immigrants and 30 emigrants.

options.text: The population grew by 420, because immigrants and births both count as additions
options.misconception: adds gains without subtracting any of the losses

options.text: The population grew by 180, because 400 plus 60 gains exceed 250 plus 30 losses
The population grew by 400, because the birth total is the only count that matters
options.misconception: ignores deaths and movement entirely

options.text: The population fell by 30, because the deaths outweighed the births in the colony
options.misconception: compares only births with deaths and ignores movement

questions.explanation: Gains of 400 births plus 60 immigrants total 460, and losses of 250 deaths plus 30 emigrants total 280, giving a net increase of 180 mice. All components must be included for the accounting to hold.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State what limits the fraction of energy transferred between levels
questions.stem: A survey team explains why a marsh supports far fewer herons than the reeds they sit among.

options.text: Only a small share of the energy at one level becomes biomass at the next level up
Most of the reed's energy is bound in cellulose that herons cannot digest or reach
options.misconception: explains a low transfer by the wrong physical barrier

options.text: Reeds reproduce slowly, so they cannot supply enough young herons each year
options.misconception: links a producer breeding to the number of top consumers

options.text: Herons leave the marsh each winter, so they are rarely present to feed on the reeds
options.misconception: explains low numbers by seasonal absence of the consumer

questions.explanation: Only about a tenth of the energy at one level becomes biomass at the next, because much is used in metabolism or lost as heat. Low consumer numbers follow from that.
questions.hint: Think about the share of energy that becomes new biomass.

questions.stem: A grassland plot survey recorded 1,200 grams of plant dry matter per square metre per year while plant respiration used 400 grams. What was the net primary productivity in grams per square metre per year?

questions.learningObjective: Explain how to reconstruct lower-level energy from a top-level figure
questions.stem: A survey team has 4,000 kilojoules at the top of a grassland chain and wants the producer level.

options.text: The producer level holds 4,000 kilojoules, since the chain conserves energy from end to end
options.misconception: assumes energy is conserved along a food chain

options.text: The producer level holds 400 kilojoules, since each transfer upward divides the energy by ten
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the pyramid calculation

options.text: The producer level holds 40 kilojoules, since most energy is lost before the top level
options.misconception: applies a loss factor in the wrong direction

options.text: The producer level holds 4,000,000 kilojoules, since three transfers each multiply the figure by ten

questions.explanation: Working backward from the top means undoing three transfers of about a tenth each, so each step down multiplies by ten. From 4,000 kilojoules that gives 4,000,000 kilojoules at the producer level.
questions.hint: Undo each ten percent step by multiplying by ten.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a food web with many links per species
questions.stem: A survey of a salt marsh finds 7 species joined by 21 feeding links, and the same number of species in a fen joined by only 6 links.

options.text: The two webs are equivalent, because species richness is the only measure of a web
options.misconception: treats species richness as the sole measure of a web

options.text: The fen is more fragile, because a simple web has no alternative energy pathway at all
options.misconception: assumes a simple web has no redundancy whatsoever

options.text: The marsh web is more complex and buffered, since more links mean more alternative pathways
The fen is richer, because a smaller web with fewer links holds more species
options.misconception: reads a lower link count as greater productivity

questions.explanation: The marsh web averages three links per species against one in the fen, so it has more alternative routes for energy. That redundancy buffers species when a link fails.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Classify surveyed limiting events by their density dependence
questions.stem: A field team lists four events that reduced a beetle population and asks which is density independent.

options.text: A parasitic wasp species that found the colony once the tunnels were well used
options.misconception: links a parasite to the density of its host population

options.text: A prolonged drought that dried the damp soil the beetles burrowed into
A fungal infection spreading faster as the remaining beetles crowded together
options.misconception: mistakes disease spread for an independent event

options.text: Scarce food causing the beetles to compete more fiercely for what was left
options.misconception: treats competition for a limited resource as independent

questions.explanation: A drought acts on the beetles whatever their density, so it is density independent. Infection, competition and parasites strengthen as the population densifies, so they are density dependent.
questions.hint: Ask whether the event needed a crowded population to work.

questions.learningObjective: Express a population count as a share of its carrying capacity
questions.stem: A survey counted 900 birds in a marsh whose carrying capacity for the species is 1,500 birds. What percentage of the carrying capacity does the population represent?
questions.explanation: The share of carrying capacity is 900 divided by 1,500, which is 0.6, or 60 percent of the limit. A population at 60 percent of capacity still has unused resources and can keep growing.
questions.hint: Divide the count by capacity and convert to a percentage.

questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a claimed population trend can be sustained
questions.stem: A report says a reintroduced hare population can keep doubling every year in the new reserve.

options.text: The claim is limited, because the population must slow as it nears the habitat's capacity
The claim holds, since released animals have no natural enemies in a new range
options.misconception: assumes absence of predators removes every limit

options.text: The claim holds, because doubling is a measured fact from the first three years
options.misconception: extrapolates a short-term rate to unlimited time

options.text: The claim is limited, because doubling always stops once the population reaches 100 animals
options.misconception: invents a fixed numerical limit for any population

questions.explanation: Logistic growth cannot continue at a constant proportional rate, because competition slows the population as it nears the reserve capacity. The early doublings are real, but the curve must flatten.
questions.hint: Consider what happens as the population nears the limit.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Determine the dominant term in a population balance
questions.stem: A surveyed vole population shows 800 young produced, 500 deaths from predation, 200 deaths of old age and 100 emigrated.

options.text: The population is stable, because births and deaths balance out over the year
options.misconception: ignores emigration when judging the balance

options.text: The population grew strongly, because 800 young is the largest single figure in the data
options.misconception: reads one large term as the whole balance

options.text: The population fell, because predation removed far more animals than were born
options.misconception: compares one loss category against all the gains

options.text: The population grew slightly, because 800 young against 700 losses leaves a small surplus

questions.explanation: Total gains of 800 young match total losses of 500 plus 200 plus 100, which is 800, so the balance is exactly zero rather than a surplus. Figures must be summed by gains and losses before comparison.

questions.learningObjective: Describe how logistic growth differs from exponential growth
questions.stem: A biologist contrasts the growth of a reintroduced herd with the growth of a laboratory culture of the same species.

options.text: The herd will keep doubling, because open ground removes all density-dependent limits
options.misconception: believes open ground removes competition entirely

options.text: Both will double forever, because doubling is what populations always do
options.misconception: generalises one growth pattern to all cases

options.text: The herd slows near its limit, while the culture keeps doubling without a natural ceiling
The herd doubles faster than the culture, because wild animals grow more quickly
options.misconception: assumes wild growth is always faster than captive growth

questions.explanation: A fed laboratory culture has no natural carrying capacity, so it can grow exponentially for long periods. A wild herd faces competition and other density-dependent limits, so growth flattens.
questions.hint: Ask which population faces a natural ceiling.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compute net population change from births and all losses
questions.stem: A vole population produced 900 young, lost 450 to predation, 150 to disease and 100 to emigration in one year. What was the net change in the population?
questions.explanation: The young produced add 900, while losses total 450 plus 150 plus 100, which is 700, so the population gains 200 net individuals. The starting count is excluded because this is a change, not a total.
questions.hint: Subtract the total losses from the number of young produced.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how emigration alters a local population count
questions.stem: A count of moths on a small hill top fell after the habitat was fenced and disturbed nearby.

options.text: Emigration reduced the count, because the fence and disturbance pushed moths off the hill
The moths left because the fence blocked their flight route to the main breeding area
options.misconception: invents a specific cause with no evidence in the survey

options.text: The moths died on the hill, because a fence always kills the moths that touch it
options.misconception: treats a barrier as a direct cause of death

options.text: The count fell because moths hide during the day and were surveyed at the wrong time
options.misconception: reaches for an unrecorded survey artefact

questions.explanation: Emigration removes individuals from a local population without killing them, so the count falls while the moths survive elsewhere. Fencing and disturbance are plausible causes of that movement.
questions.hint: Distinguish leaving the site from dying on it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Use complete accounting to judge whether a population is stable
questions.stem: Survey totals for a hillside rabbit population are 1,100 births, 950 deaths, 140 immigrants and 90 emigrants.

options.text: The population is stable, because births and deaths are almost the same number
options.misconception: compares only births with deaths and ignores movement

options.text: The population grew by 200, because the immigrant total was simply added to the births
options.misconception: adds a gain without subtracting the matching losses

options.text: The population grew by 150, since 1,100 plus 140 gains exceed 950 plus 90 losses
The population fell, because the emigration figure exceeded the immigration figure
options.misconception: compares two movement terms and ignores the rest

questions.explanation: Gains of 1,100 births plus 140 immigrants total 1,240, and losses of 950 deaths plus 90 emigrants total 1,040, leaving a net gain of 200 rabbits. Movement terms nearly cancel but must be counted.
questions.hint: Total every gain and every loss before comparing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a producer supports fewer consumers than its own biomass
questions.stem: A marsh survey finds abundant reeds but relatively few insects feeding on them.

options.text: The insects are absent because the reeds outcompeted them for space in the marsh
options.misconception: assumes a producer competes with consumers for space

options.text: Most reed energy is spent on cellulose that the insects cannot break down
The insects are absent because the reeds block sunlight from the water they live in
options.misconception: explains consumer scarcity by light rather than energy

options.text: The insects are absent because reed beds provide no shelter from wind for them
options.misconception: invents a shelter effect that the survey never recorded

questions.explanation: Much of a reed energy sits in cellulose and lignin that many insects cannot digest, so only a small share reaches them. Trophic efficiency is low for the same reason transfers between levels are low.
questions.hint: Think about which part of a plant is actually edible.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate net primary productivity when a second loss is present
questions.stem: A wetland plot survey measured 900 grams of dry matter per square metre per year, 300 grams used in plant respiration and 100 grams eaten by herbivores. What was the net primary productivity in grams per square metre per year?
questions.explanation: Net primary productivity counts only the loss to plant respiration, so 900 minus 300 gives 600 grams per square metre per year. The 100 grams eaten by herbivores are a later transfer between levels.
questions.hint: Subtract plant respiration, and leave herbivory out of it.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about pyramid direction when reconstructing energy
questions.stem: A survey team wants to check a pyramid that lists 90 kilojoules at the top and 900,000 at the base.

options.text: The pyramid is plausible, because working back three steps from the top gives the base
The pyramid is impossible, because the base must be exactly ten times the level above it
options.misconception: treats the ten percent rule as an exact ratio

options.text: The pyramid is impossible, because energy always decreases upward in a real pyramid
options.misconception: confuses rule direction with number direction

options.text: The pyramid is impossible, because a real pyramid must hold more species at the base
options.misconception: checks energy against a rule about species counts

questions.explanation: Working back from 90 kilojoules at the top gives 900, then 9,000, then 90,000 at the base over three steps, so 900,000 is one step high. The rule is approximate, so that shape is not ruled out.
questions.hint: Work backward from the top and count the steps.

questions.learningObjective: Read a species and link count as evidence of web complexity
questions.stem: A survey of two ponds finds 5 species and 8 links in the first, and 5 species and 20 links in the second.

options.text: The first pond is more complex, because simpler webs are easier for predators to exploit
options.misconception: equates simplicity with greater complexity

options.text: Both ponds are equally complex, because they contain the same number of species
options.misconception: uses species richness as the only measure of complexity

options.text: Neither pond can be ranked, because link counts cannot be compared between habitats
options.misconception: claims the counts are not comparable at all

options.text: The second pond is more complex, because it has more links between the same species

questions.explanation: With the same number of species in both ponds, the one with four links per species is the more complex web, because more of its species feed on several things, giving energy more alternative routes.
questions.hint: Compare links per species rather than species counts.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify an independent cause behind a population decline
questions.stem: A field biologist reports a sharp fall in a vole population the spring after an unusually wet winter.

options.text: Competition for grain in the fields intensified as the population became denser
options.misconception: chooses a crowding explanation for a seasonal event

options.text: Disease spread through the colony as the survivors packed into the remaining dry ground
options.misconception: mistakes crowding-related disease for an independent factor

options.text: The wet winter flooded the burrows and drowned nesting females regardless of density
Parasitic worms found the colony because the wet winter concentrated them in the burrows
options.misconception: links a parasite to a seasonal event

questions.explanation: Flooding acts on the voles whatever their density, so it is density independent, and the timing fits the wet winter. Competition, disease and parasites depend on crowding, so they fit another pattern.
questions.hint: Ask whether the cause needed a crowded population to act.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage of carrying capacity in use
questions.stem: A rocky shore survey found 240 limpets per square metre, and that shore can support 800 per square metre. What percentage of the carrying capacity is being used?
questions.explanation: The share of capacity in use is 240 divided by 800, which is 0.3, or 30 percent of the limit. A population using under half of its capacity still has room to grow before density-dependent limits bite.
questions.hint: Divide the count by capacity and convert to a percentage.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Judge the effect of removing a density-dependent limit
questions.stem: A farmer argues that removing crows from his field will let the vole population grow without limit.

options.text: The argument is sound, because vole numbers are usually set by predators alone
options.misconception: assumes a single factor sets the population size

options.text: The argument is flawed, because removing crows leaves food, space and disease as further limits
The argument is sound, because crows are the only limit on a vole population
options.misconception: treats one predator as the only possible limit

options.text: The argument is flawed, because removing crows will make the voles stop reproducing
options.misconception: invents a reproductive effect of predator removal

questions.explanation: Crows are one density-dependent limit among several, and food, space, disease and other predators still act on the voles. Removing one check may let numbers rise, but a capacity still applies.
questions.hint: Ask what else is still limiting the voles.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a change in a population balance from survey totals
questions.stem: A survey of a ground squirrel colony records 2,400 young born, 1,500 deaths, 200 immigrants and 100 emigrants in one year.

options.text: The colony shrank, because 1,500 deaths outweighed the single birth figure
options.misconception: compares one loss term against all the gains

options.text: The colony doubled, because 2,400 young were produced during the year
options.misconception: uses a raw birth count as a growth factor

options.text: The colony stayed level, because births and emigration happened to be similar numbers
options.misconception: compares two unrelated terms to call the change zero

options.text: The colony grew by 1,000, since 2,600 gains exceed 1,600 losses

questions.explanation: Gains of 2,400 young plus 200 immigrants total 2,600, and losses of 1,500 deaths plus 100 emigrants total 1,600, so the colony increased by 1,000. Growth is always the difference between the totals.
questions.hint: Add all gains, add all losses, then subtract.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a survey design can hide migration effects
questions.stem: A survey plan for a coastal valley relies on one count point at the valley floor each September.

options.text: Counts are unreliable, because birds that move between the count point and the hills are missed
Counts are reliable, because one well-placed point sees every bird that uses the valley
options.misconception: assumes a single point captures a whole valley population

options.text: Counts are reliable, because migration in and out of a valley is negligible in autumn
options.misconception: assumes migration is always small in a valley system

options.text: Counts are unreliable, because bird numbers always change most between two autumn counts
options.misconception: invents a seasonal pattern that the survey never recorded

questions.explanation: A single count point samples only the birds that use that spot, and birds shifting between the valley floor and hills are missed. Movement like that means the count misses the population.
questions.hint: Ask what a single point can and cannot sample.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compute an end-of-year count including births, deaths and migration
questions.stem: A deer survey counted 340 deer at the start of the year; 52 fawns were born, 28 deer died and 35 immigrated. How many deer were counted at the end of the year?
questions.explanation: From 340 deer, adding 52 births and 35 immigrants and subtracting 28 deaths gives 399 deer at year end. Emigration is not listed, so the record must note that no movement losses were seen.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a proposal to change a web's energy transfer
questions.stem: A fishery officer proposes adding a plank-eating fish to raise the total catch of predatory fish.

options.text: The plan is sound, because extra food at the base always raises every level above it
options.misconception: assumes a producer addition lifts all levels without cost

options.text: The plan is sound, because the new fish would simply replace the fish already there
options.misconception: assumes a new feeder causes no change in the rest of the web

options.text: The plan is doubtful, because the new fish compete with existing plank feeders for the same food
The plan is doubtful, because plank-eating fish always destroy the predators that feed on them
options.misconception: invents a destructive effect on the predators

questions.explanation: Adding a plank eater inserts a new consumer drawing on the same limited plankton, so it competes with existing plank feeders. Whether the predator catch rises depends on how that competition balances.
questions.hint: Ask what the new fish and the existing feeders share.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a productivity figure against the respiration of the plants
questions.stem: A forest floor survey records 2,000 grams of litter per square metre per year and 1,100 grams of green plant material produced.

options.text: Net primary productivity is 1,100 grams, since that is the material the trees built
options.misconception: reports gross production as the net figure

options.text: Net primary productivity is 900 grams, which is production after the plants respired
Net primary productivity is 3,100 grams, since litter and green material are both new production
options.misconception: adds a consumer loss to the producer production figure

options.text: Net primary productivity is 2,000 grams, because the litter total is the plant production
options.misconception: mistakes litter input for plant production

questions.explanation: Net primary productivity is the green material produced minus what the plants respire, so 1,100 minus 200 gives 900 grams per square metre per year. Litter passes to decomposers, not into net output.
questions.hint: Net production subtracts the plants respiratory loss.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Select the correct scale factor when moving down a pyramid
questions.stem: A survey of a heathland pyramid puts 250 kilojoules at the level of heather and wants the spiders above it.

options.text: About 250,000 kilojoules, since each step up the pyramid multiplies the energy by ten
options.misconception: applies the pyramid rule in the upward direction

options.text: About 2,500 kilojoules, since the spider level holds more energy than the plants
options.misconception: asserts energy rises as it moves up the pyramid

options.text: About 25 kilojoules, since the spiders take a tenth of what the heather supports
About 2.5 kilojoules, since the spiders gain only a hundredth of the plant energy
options.misconception: applies a hundredfold transfer instead of tenfold

questions.explanation: Moving one step up from heather to spiders means only about a tenth of the energy is transferred, so 250 kilojoules at heather supports about 25 kilojoules of spiders. Energy always falls upward.
questions.hint: One step up divides the energy by about ten.

questions.stem: A grassland food web was charted with 14 feeding links between 7 recorded species. What is the mean number of feeding links per species?

questions.learningObjective: Compare two candidate causes using density dependence
questions.stem: A field team has two explanations for a bird decline: a hard winter and a rise in a nest parasite.

options.text: The winter fits the data better, because a severe winter hits every density of birds alike
Both fits equally, because no survey can separate weather from parasitism
options.misconception: declines to weigh any of the available evidence

options.misconception: asserts that declines never happen in a single season

questions.learningObjective: Assess a claim that a population is near its limit
questions.stem: Survey counts of a shrub vole population stand at 5,000, and the estimated carrying capacity of the meadow is 12,000.

options.text: The population is at capacity, because 5,000 voles is a large number for a meadow
options.misconception: judges abundance without comparing it to capacity

options.text: The population is over capacity, because the meadow cannot hold more than 5,000 voles
options.misconception: invents a capacity figure that was never given

options.text: The population is at capacity, because the counts have not changed since the first survey
options.misconception: reads a single stable count as a ceiling

options.text: The population is well below capacity, so it should keep growing for now

questions.explanation: At 5,000 against a capacity of 12,000 the population is at about 42 percent of the limit, so resources remain and the count can keep rising. A number only means something when compared with capacity.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise the point at which growth begins to slow
questions.stem: A biologist watches a rising population of introduced rabbits on an island.

options.misconception: assumes a food crash always happens every year

options.text: Growth slows as the island nears the number of rabbits it can support

options.misconception: claims reproduction stops entirely under crowding

questions.explanation: As a population nears the number the habitat can support, competition for space and food intensifies and growth slows. Reproduction continues but fewer young are added per adult, flattening the curve.

questions.stem: A seabird island held 900 adult birds at the start of the season, produced 1,250 fledged chicks, and lost 380 adults and 90 birds to emigration. How many birds were on the island at the end of the season?
